content:
Would there be interest in having Schoof's theorem in Mathlib.

I was thinking about formalising this series up to chapter 8.
Do you mean Schoof’s algorithm? He has many theorems, e.g, on abelian varieties with restricted bad reduction.
Yes, the algorithm that counts the number of points of an elliptic curve over a finite field.

Well reading the chapter makes me deeply worried.

I can't find any definitions that I can build upon. Neither Isogeny is defined, nor plane projective curve, the best here is this. How hard would it to define the multiplication by 2 isogeny and to prove that is has degree 4? I can understand the general idea of the calculation, so once the definitions are in it should be fine, but I don't know which way would be the most general way. I can see that there are some definitions regarding Projective are defined as schemes and this appears to have some semblance to Definition 4.2, but this is way too much abstract nonsense for me.

Can anyone point me in the right direction with what to start?

Re proving that multiplication by 2 has degree 4 -- what is your proposed decfinition of degree? There are several and it's not trivial to relate them, and I'm pretty sure that we don't have any in mathlib.
We have that multiplication by 2 in a char =/= 2 separably closed field has 4 points in the kernel somewhere in Lean (not mathlib)
@Andrew Yang has thought of Schoof a while back but I don’t know the status of it

TL;DR: I need definitions that allow the bounds of Schoof's algorithm to work.

So my goal is to prove concrete properties about elliptic curves used in cryptography, including how long the orbits are.

I want to prove Schoof's algorithm, given a finite field of characteristic p > 3, and a bunch of computational hypotheses that the number of points is equal to some chinese remainder theorem.

I've briefly glanced at the proof and some but not all of its dependencies. The trace of a Frobenius, Hasse, Division polynomials, Chinese Remainder Theorem, the sum with an inseperable isogeny is separable iff the other summand is separable. Some of those are already in mathlib.

Degree of an isogeny seems to be defined as the maximum of the degrees of the numerator and denominator in standard form.

And then likely something to relate the degree and the number of points on a curve.

My main focus is contributing to mathlib and building the API, with a nice side effect of learning about elliptic curves and a bit of "modern" algebraic geometry.

Where would I optimally start?

It's all well and good saying "degree of an isogeny is X and also Y", the issue is that there are several definitions and it's some work to relate them. But I think more of an issue will be the Hasse bounds, which are a crucial part of the argument. These are delicate and although there are some hack proofs which work in special cases, mathlib would want the general proof which works for all finite fields and is a crucial ingredient in proving the algorithm is correct. Are you sorrying these or proving them?
@Chris Birkbeck is working on the Hasse bound
Yeah hopefully I'll have something concrete to say about this soon, but it's not ready yet.
I should also say we also want isogenies for the LMFDB project, so if anyone else wants to work on that I'd be happy to coordinate.
Is the idea to continue develop things for the Weierstrass model or to do everything for schemes and then somehow specialize?

For now I was just thinking elliptic curves since one thing we want are the LMFDB labels for elliptic curves. But I guess one could also make a general definition for group schemes and then leave the gluing until we have more API for viewing elliptic curves as schemes.

@Kevin Buzzard I'm afraid I'm not that competent in wading through the intricacies of proper definitions but if an expert points me to the right directions I could probably fill the sorries and develop the library that way.

Tbf I wasn't really happy with the linked literature, it doesn't go in full generality and it skips lots of steps.

For example I could find multiple definitions of isogenies over algebraic varieties and the specialisation over elliptic curves, and even there there are at least two definitions that have a nontrivial (and referenceless) relationship between them.

Looking into mathlib I couldn't find the definition of algebraic variety. Does mathlib use schemes for that?

@Chris Birkbeck what would the plan be here?

It sounds like the plan is not to use varieties (which are a special case of schemes) at all and to continue to develop theory for Weierstrass curves ie cubic equations. Yes there are several definitions but they're all the same and the proofs are there if you know where to look :-)
